analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to accommodate menopause symptoms like hot flashes and sleep disruption at work.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 7 cosponsors, has sat in four House committees with no hearing, markup, or vote since July 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require employers with 15 or more workers to provide reasonable accommodations to employees experiencing menopause symptoms — for example, letting a worker keep water at her station, take extra restroom breaks, or alternate sitting and standing — with exceptions only for undue hardship. It borrows the structure of the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act: workers who ask for help get protections, medical information stays confidential, retaliation is banned, and violations can be enforced through the EEOC with the same remedies as Title VII. It also covers congressional, federal, and state employees. As of now it has only been referred to four committees and no committee has acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Women in the menopausal transition and menopause — the bill's findings note women ages 45 to 64 are over 17 percent of the U.S. labor force — plus all workers who might one day need these accommodations, and applicants as well as current employees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women workers in midlife and later

how_it_helps.text: Requires covered employers to reasonably accommodate known menopause-related limitations unless doing so imposes an undue hardship, and defines 'known limitation' broadly to include hot flashes, sleep disruption, dizziness, cognitive issues, fatigue, and urinary symptoms [S2].

Creates a presumption that four simple accommodations — keeping water nearby, extra restroom breaks, sitting or standing as needed, and breaks to eat and drink — are reasonable and should not require documentation [S2].

Bans forcing a worker onto paid or unpaid leave when another accommodation is available, bans retaliation against workers who request accommodations, and requires menopause-related medical information be kept confidential [S2].

Enforces the right through EEOC procedures and damages modeled on Title VII and the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, and extends the same protections to congressional, federal, and state employees [S2].
Requires the EEOC to issue implementing regulations within one year of enactment, and appropriates $4.5 million to carry out the Act [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers with 15 or more employees — private businesses, plus congressional offices, federal agencies, and state governments — who bear the cost of providing accommodations, adjusting schedules and duties, and possible damages in enforcement actions.

drawbacks.text: Employers must provide the accommodations at their own expense and, for the four 'Predictable Assessment' items, cannot demand medical documentation even when requesting verification of a condition, which removes an individualized check on requests [S2].

The list of covered symptoms is long — including mood changes, anxiety, depression, dry skin, and headaches — and the bill directs courts not to spend 'extensive analysis or documentation' on whether a worker qualifies, which could broaden the population of covered requests and generate disputes over what is reasonable [S2].

Damages are barred when an employer can show good-faith efforts, in consultation with the employee, to find an equally effective accommodation, so the remedy is weaker than a straight anti-discrimination suit when an employer tries but fails to accommodate [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accommodations in question — water, bathroom breaks, a place to sit — are modest and the bill lets employers escape them for undue hardship, so the burden on most businesses is small compared with the benefit of keeping experienced midlife workers on the job. The real design trade-offs are the presumption against documentation and the very broad symptom list, which lean the enforcement burden toward employers. The bill also protects its own interest by capping damages for employers who make good-faith accommodation efforts. On balance it is a targeted workplace-rights bill, not a sweeping mandate, and no substantive objection appeared in the record.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2026 and sent to four House committees, but no committee has held a hearing or markup and the House has not voted on it; the Congress runs through January 3, 2027.

narrative.text: Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-MI) introduced H.R. 9671 on July 14, 2026, joined by Reps. Clarke (NY), Norton, Wilson (FL), and Tlaib [S2].

The Speaker referred the bill to four committees — Education and Workforce, House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, and Judiciary — for consideration of the provisions under each committee's jurisdiction [S4].
Seven House Democrats cosponsored the bill [S3].
No further action — hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — has been recorded since the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has lost or gained directly. Covered employers avoid any new accommodation obligation as long as the bill stalls; women workers get nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, so far, avoid the mandate

for.name: Rep. Debbie Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill with four original cosponsors

against.name: House committees (Education and Workforce, House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, Judiciary)
against.what_they_did: No committee has scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill since its July 2026 referral

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats sponsored and cosponsored the bill, but no Republican has publicly opposed it and no vote has been held, so the partisan shape of the outcome is not yet established.

industries.note: The bill requires these employers to provide menopause-related accommodations and creates enforcement exposure with damages, at a cost they currently do not bear. The interest in avoiding that obligation runs directly against the workers who would get the accommodations.

analysis.trajectory: A minority-party bill with seven cosponsors, referred to four committees in the closing months of a two-year Congress, would ordinarily need a committee to schedule it before the House could vote; nothing suggests any committee intends to. Barring an unexpected markup, the bill is likely to expire at the end of this Congress without a vote.
